HENRY FORD, MY LIFE AND WORK (1923) 1

The technological revolution received a huge boost from the work of Henry Ford. In his autobiography, My Life and Work , he describes how he dramatically increased efficiency through the specialization of work and constant innovation. By producing vastly more cars per worker, the Ford Motor Company was able to double the average wage to $5.00 per day, which enabled many of his employees to purchase Fords, even as their cost

...

s now divided into eighty-four operations—those men do the work that three times their number formerly did. In a short time we tried out the plan on the chassis.

...

We tried the experiment of drawing the chassis with a rope and windlass down a line two hundred fifty feet long. Six assemblers traveled with the chassis and picked up the parts from piles

1 Henry Ford, with Samuel Crowther, My Life and Work (Garden City, NY: Doubleday, Page & Co.,. 1923), 81-90.

2

placed along the line. This rough experiment reduced the time to five hours fifty minutes per chassis. In the early part of 1914 we elevated the assembly line. We had adopted the policy of "man-high" work; we had one line twenty-six and three quarter inches and another twenty-four and one half inches from the floor—to suit squads of different heights. The waist-high arrangement and a further subdivision of work so that each man had fewer movements cut down the labour time per chassis to one hour thirty-three minutes.
